# The Age of Human Comparison With AI: Development of AI Competence Anxiety Scale and AI Optimism Scale and Their Relationship With Generative AI Literacy and AI Self-Efficacy

1. Introduction

In recent years, the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) systems has led to their integration into various fields, including healthcare, education, and psychology. According to Statista ([2024)](#about-the-authors), the number of AI users reached 374 million in the first quarter of 2025, with a forecasted increase to 1.2 billion by 2031. Although AI technologies assist with big data analysis, the personalization of learning, the accessibility of information, and the generation of alternative solutions, they also pose risks related to deepfakes, dehumanization, data privacy violations, information distortion, and ethical violations (Sharma, [2024)](#about-the-authors). The swift and unpredictable development of AI systems has elicited a range of emo- tional responses, from excitement and curiosity to uncertainty, fear, and anxiety (Farrow, 2021). Research has shown that concerns about replacement by AI, uncontrolled growth of AI, privacy issues, AI-generated misinformation, and AI bias contribute to anxiety regarding these systems (Hong, 2025; Kim et al., 2025).

### AI anxiety refers to differences between individuals in the probability of experiencing tension, appre- hension, and worry with physiological arousal when anticipating potential negative consequences of AI (Hong, 2025). It is also defined as a general emotional response characterized by anxiety or fear that

hinders engagement with AI (Wang & Wang, [2022)](#about-the-authors). The components of AI anxiety include learning (i.e., concerns about learning AI technologies), job replacement (i.e., concerns that AI technologies will replace human jobs), sociotechnical blindness (i.e., concerns about neglecting the social, ethical, and technical risks associated with AI), and AI configuration (i.e., concerns about perceiving AI systems as confusing) (Wang & Wang, [2022)](#about-the-authors). Although these components and hidden catalysts of AI anxiety (Kim et al., 2025) have been proposed, the individual’s feelings of inadequacy about their own compe- tence with AI technologies have often been overlooked. To address this gap, we introduced the concept of AI competence anxiety, defined as the anxiety arising from perceiving one’s own competence as insufficient compared to AI technologies.

Building on this conceptualization, it is important to consider how the rapid advancement of AI impacts individuals’ perceptions of their own competence. The progress of AI across multiple domains has led individuals to critically reflect on their own skills and abilities (Li & Huang, 2020). The increas- ing proficiency of AI in problem-solving (Mohamed et al., 2024), creativity (Ding & Li, 2025), and crit- ical thinking (Gerlich, 2025) encourages individuals to compare their capabilities with to those of AI, leading to concerns about whether their competencies are sufficient. According to comparison theory, individuals assess their competence by referencing others; when they perceive themselves as less adequate or capable, they experience anxiety (Festinger, 1954). As AI technologies continue to grow in capacity and skill, such comparisons increase, fueling fears that AI systems may exceed their capabil- ities, triggering doubts that one’s own skills may become trivial, ultimately contributing to AI compe- tence anxiety. Such anxiety may have detrimental outcomes, such as increased stress and reduced engagement with AI. Therefore, it is crucial to identify factors that alleviate AI competence anxiety in order to develop effective strategies for its mitigation and prevention. In this context, the current study proposes a model that examines the mediating roles of AI self-efficacy and AI optimism in the associ- ation between Generative AI (GenAI) literacy and AI competence anxiety.

Considering the influence of AI competence anxiety on individuals’ engagement with AI, it is crucial to examine literacy in emerging AI technologies, particularly Generative AI (GenAI). GenAI is a type of AI that produces new, creative, and original products (Feuerriegel et al., 2024). GenAI literacy is defined as the individual’s ability to identify, comprehend, appropriately use, evaluate, and apply GenAI within ethical boundaries (Annapureddy et al., [2025)](#ethical-approval). Its components include awareness (i.e., recognizing and understanding GenAI), usage (i.e., using GenAI effectively), evaluation (i.e., assessing its strengths and weaknesses), and ethics (i.e., using GenAI responsibly and sensitively within ethical boundaries) (Gokc€ ¸earslan et al., 2024; Wang et al., [2023)](#about-the-authors). GenAI strengthens prompt skills and fosters competence in the use of AI technologies (Gibreel & Arpaci, 2025). Recognizing GenAI, understanding its responsible and informed use, and being aware of its potential risks can help mitigate uncertainty and apprehension toward AI (Schiavo et al., 2024).

Previous studies have reported a negative association between AI literacy and AI anxiety in different samples. For example, Cengiz and Peker ([2025)](#ethical-approval) found that among university students, higher accept- ance of generative AI was linked to lower levels of AI anxiety. Their findings also showed that AI liter- acy and positive attitudes toward AI sequentially mediated this relationship, indicating that both greater acceptance of AI and improved AI literacy can play a role in reducing anxiety about using AI technologies. Pan et al. (2025) reported similar findings among academics and postgraduate students, showing that higher AI literacy was associated with lower AI anxiety and influenced their behavioral intentions toward AI-assisted literature reading. Ozc€ ¸evik-Subas¸i et al. (2024) found that among pediat- ric nurses, higher AI literacy was associated with lower AI anxiety, and more positive attitudes toward AI were linked to higher AI literacy and lower anxiety. In addition, a study with pre-service teachers showed that 10.3% of AI anxiety could be predicted by the technical sub-dimension of digital literacy, suggesting that greater technical digital fluency reduces concerns about AI (Aydug & Altınpulluk, [2025)](#ethical-approval). Schiavo et al. (2024) examined how individuals’ AI literacy and anxiety influence their attitudes toward accepting AI technologies. Their findings suggest that while higher AI literacy promotes a posi- tive attitude toward AI acceptance, anxiety exerts a small but significant direct negative effect and also serves as an important mediator of literacy’s influence. Although these studies have emphasized the negative relationship between AI literacy and AI anxiety, the factors underlying the relationship

INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF HUMAN–COMPUTER INTERACTION 3

between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety remain unclear. The current study suggests that GenAI literacy may reduce AI competence anxiety through AI self-efficacy and AI optimism.

2. AI self-efficacy and AI optimism as serial mediators

AI self-efficacy is defined as the belief in one’s ability to learn, use, and manage AI technologies (Wang & Chuang, [2024)](#about-the-authors). The social cognitive theory, which sets out the antecedents and consequences of self- efficacy, suggests that an individual’s confidence in their own capacity and ability in a specific area alle- viates anxiety (Bandura, [1988)](#ethical-approval). Accordingly, perceived competence in using AI technologies serves as a buffer against AI-related anxiety (Bewersdorff et al., [2025)](#ethical-approval) Furthermore, individuals’ confidence and ease in using these technologies contribute to lowering AI anxiety (Chen et al., [2024a)](#ethical-approval). Wang et al. ([2024)](#about-the-authors) found that among pre-service teachers, technology self-efficacy reduced GenAI anxiety while positively influencing effort expectancy, performance expectancy, and GenAI TPACK, which in turn shaped their behavioral intentions to design GenAI-assisted teaching. Similarly, Chen et al. (2024b) conducted a study with university students focusing on the use of AI in L2 learning. Their findings indicated that AI self-efficacy not only reduces AI anxiety but also fosters more positive attitudes toward AI and encourages greater use of AI tools. Additionally, the research showed that AI self- efficacy promotes AI use both directly and indirectly by lowering anxiety and enhancing attitudes. Based on these previous findings, this study expects that higher AI self-efficacy is associated with lower AI competence anxiety.

Grounded in social cognitive theory, the idea that both direct and indirect learning can enhance self- efficacy, leading to reduced anxiety (Bandura, [1988)](#ethical-approval), is particularly relevant in the context of AI. In this setting, AI literacy helps individuals develop technological competencies more easily and effectively (Annapureddy et al., [2025)](#ethical-approval). Awareness of AI technologies, that is understanding their strengths and weaknesses, critically evaluating them, and recognizing potential ethical violations, promotes AI self- efficacy (Becirovic et al., [2025)](#ethical-approval). AI literacy helps foster a positive attitude toward AI by enabling individ- uals to use AI systems effectively, understand the ethical boundaries of AI technologies, adopt a critical approach to these systems, and remain aware of both their benefits and potential harms (Boztepe et al., [2025)](#ethical-approval). GenAI awareness is essential for benefiting from AI technologies and recognizing their potential harms (Semerci S¸ahin et al., [2025)](#about-the-authors). GenAI enhances individuals’ professional knowledge, learning ease, and skills, thereby strengthening their self-efficacy (Durmus¸ Sarıkahya et al., 2025). Empirical studies support this notion. For instance, a study with university students from three countries examined how AI usage, attitudes toward AI, and AI literacy contribute to AI self-efficacy. The results indicated that AI usage and positive attitudes significantly predicted interest in AI, and AI literacy was positively asso- ciated with AI self-efficacy, with interest in AI further enhancing self-efficacy (Bewersdorff et al., [2025)](#ethical-approval). Additionally, individuals’ belief and trust in their competence to use AI technologies reduce their anxiety about AI (Chen et al., 2024b). In this context, GenAI literacy may reduce AI competence anxiety by fos- tering AI self-efficacy. Put differently, AI self-efficacy may mediate the relationship between GenAI liter- acy and AI competence anxiety.

In addition to AI self-efficacy, AI optimism may also mediate between GenAI literacy and AI com- petence anxiety. Optimism is generally characterized by a positive attitude toward life events and expectations for the future (Scheier & Carver, 1985). In the digital context, this concept has been defined as a favorable perception of the technological advancement and positive expectations regarding future developments in technology (Prokopovic, 2017). The Technology Readiness Index emphasizes that optimism is a critical component that facilitates the proper, flexible, and competent use of new technology (Parasuraman, 2000). Following this conceptual framework, we applied the notion of opti- mism to AI, defining AI optimism as a positive perception of developments in AI technologies and an expectation of continued progress. Similar to general optimism (Scheier & Carver, 2018), focusing on the positive aspects of AI developments and maintaining positive expectations about AI progress may serve as a buffer against anxiety. Research further supports the the role of optimism in reducing anx- iety. For instance, Chu et al. (2022) demonstrated that among patients with cervical spondylosis, opti- mism was negatively associated with anxiety, with resilience mediating this relationship. Higher levels of optimism contributed to greater resilience, which in turn helped reduce anxiety. This finding is

4 B. KAYA ET AL.

further supported by an experimental study evaluating the 10-week Aussie Optimism Program–Positive Thinking Skills (AOP-PTS), which aimed to prevent anxiety and depression in middle primary school children. The study indicated that fostering optimism was associated with reduced anxiety levels (Johnstone et al., 2014). In line with these findings, systematic reviews consistently reported that opti- mism serves as a protective factor against anxiety (Fasano et al., 2020; Rincon-Uribe et al., 2022). Accordingly, positive expectations about AI and positive perceptions of AI progress may be associated with lower levels of AI competence anxiety; that is, AI optimism may be negatively related to AI com- petence anxiety.

The optimism model (Carver & Scheier, [2002)](#ethical-approval) may also provide a framework for understanding the relationship between GenAI literacy, optimism, and anxiety. According to this model, enhancing an individual’s competence and skills in a particular field supports a positive attitude and expectation about that field. Optimism shaped by positive expectations promotes positive emotions and decreases apprehension (Carver & Scheier, [2002)](#ethical-approval). In this regard, AI literacy teaches individuals practical and easy ways to utilize AI technologies, fostering a positive attitude toward AI (Laupichler et al., 2024). Empirical evidence supports this link. For instance, Chai et al. ([2024)](#ethical-approval) showed the positive association between AI learning and optimism, while Hollands and Breazeal (2024) reported that implementing an AI literacy curriculum increased students’ optimism about AI. Moreover, optimism is a critical factor in alleviating anxiety (Fasano et al., 2020). Positive expectations and positive perception help buffer anxiety (Scheier & Carver, 1985). Overall, these findings indicate that, GenAI literacy may reduce AI competence anxiety through promoting AI optimism. In other words, AI optimism is likely to mediate the relationship between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety.

Beyond separate mediating roles, AI self-efficacy and AI optimism may jointly operate in a serial mediation pathway linking generative AI literacy to AI competence anxiety. Social cognitive theory sug- gests that learning experiences enhance both self-efficacy and positive expectancy, which in turn help reduce anxiety (Bandura, [1988)](#ethical-approval). In line with this, AI literacy increases AI self-efficacy by enabling indi- viduals to recognize AI technologies, understand their benefits and limitations, and apply them effect- ively (Hornberger et al., 2025). Self-efficacy, in turn, has been shown to promote optimism by encouraging positive perceptions and expectations in specific domains (Klassen, 2004). Optimism- charactarized by positive expectations and favorable interpretations of events-has been found to allevi- ate anxiety (Johnstone et al., 2014). Taken together, these findings suggest that GenAI literacy may reduce AI competence anxiety by enhancing AI self-efficacy and AI optimism may also jointly operate in a serial mediation pathway linking GenAI literacy to AI competence anxiety.

3. The current study

Despite the growing positive perceptions and expectations surrounding AI technologies, there is still no validated scale to assess AI optimism. Moreover, although AI permeates every aspect of life and indi- viduals are concerned about their own competence relative to AI, no psychometric instrument is avail- able to measure AI competence anxiety. Accordingly, this study has three main aims. First, it seeks to develop and psychometrically analyze the Competence Anxiety Scale (AICAS); second, it aims to develop and validate the AI Optimism Scale (AIOS). Third, it investigates the serial mediating roles of AI self-efficacy and AI optimism in the association between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety. This study makes several key contributions. It introduces two psychometrically sound self-report instru- ments to measure AI optimism and AI competence anxiety, enabling researchers to explore their ante- cedents, consequences, and potential interventions. Additionally, by examining the serial mediation model, the study offers insights into how AI self-efficacy and AI optimism may jointly mitigate AI competence anxiety. These findings provide evidence for the development of targeted AI literacy-based intervention strategies for AI competence anxiety.

Until now, the absence of scales measuring AI optimism and AI competence anxiety has represented a significant gap in the literature. This study addresses this gap by developing such scales. Moreover, the mechanism linking GenAI literacy to AI competence anxiety has remained unclear. By revealing the mediating roles of AI self-efficacy and AI optimism, this study advances understanding of that mechanism and underscores its own contribution to the field. In this regard, Studies I and II focus on

INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF HUMAN–COMPUTER INTERACTION 5

the development and initial validity of AICAS while Studies III and IV address the development and initial validity of AIOS. Study V investigates the serial mediation role of AI self-efficacy and AI opti- mism in the relationship between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety. Considering the reviewed literature, the following hypotheses are suggested:

H[^1]: AICAS is psychometrically valid and reliable.

H[^2]: AIOS is psychometrically valid and reliable.

H[^3]: AI self-efficacy mediates the relationship between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety.

H[^4]: AI optimism mediates the relationship between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety.

H5: AI self-efficacy and AI optimism serially mediate the relationship between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety.

## 4. Methods

### 4.1. Study I

In this section, the AICAS was developed as a Likert-type scale to measure AI competence anxiety, drawing on comparison theory (Festinger, 1954) and following established protocols. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA), a classical test theory analysis (CTT), and the graded response model (GRM), a type of item response theory (IRT) model, were applied to evaluate its psychometric properties.

#### 4.1.3. Statistical analysis In the first step, EFA was performed. First, we checked the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) value to evalu- ate the adequacy of the sample size. A KMO value greater than 0.80 indicates that sample size is adequate (Field, 2017). Second, the eigenvalues were assessed to determine the number of factors in AICAS, ensuring that the eigenvalues were greater than 1.00 for the factor solution (Hair et al., 2014). Third, the explained variances were evaluated. The acceptance threshold for a scale is that it explains more than 40% of the variance (Tabachnick & Fidell, [2007)](#about-the-authors). Fourth, kurtosis and skewness values were analyzed to determine the normality of the items, with ±2 considered the normality criterion (George & Mallery, 2019). Fifth, factor loadings and item-total correlations of AICAS items were checked, with both required to be above 0.40 (Hair et al., 2014). Finally, Cronbach’s alpha (a), McDonald’s omega (x), and Guttmann’s lambda (k6) were examined for internal consistency. A reliability coefficient above

0.70 is an indicator of internal consistency (Field, 2017). In the second step, IRT analysis was performed. IRT is a widely used approach for scale develop-

ment. IRT assumes that a scale is unidimensional and examines the discrimination of its items, indicat- ing that items with high discrimination effectively represent the scale (Samejima, 2016). The GRM, which is one of the IRT models, is preferred for Likert scales (Baker & Kim, [2017)](#ethical-approval). To determine the discrimination of the items, low (0.01–0.64), medium (0.65–1.34), high (1.35–1.69), and very high (\>1.70) discrimination coefficient (a) (Baker, [2001)](#ethical-approval), criteria were considered. In addition, boundary characteristic curves visualize the discrimination of the items (Baker & Kim, [2017)](#ethical-approval).

#### 4.1.4. Results The kurtosis values of the item ranged from −1.17 and −0.67, and the skewness values ranged from −0.08 and −0.48, indicating a normal distribution. First, EFA was conducted. Since the Kaiser-Meyer- Olkin value was 0.89, indicating that the sample size was sufficient for the seven-item pool. A single- factor structure for the AICAS was accepted, with an eigenvalue of 4.97 for the first factor and 0.58 to

0.15 for the second and subsequent factors. This single-factor structure explained 70.93% variance. Factor loadings ranged from 0.79 and 0.89, commonalities ranged from 0.63 and 0.79, and item-total correlations ranged from 0.72 and 0.84. The scree plot also supported a single-factor solution. The internal consistency was obtained as a ¼ 0.93, x ¼ 0.93, and k6 ¼ 0.93. 4.2. Study II

In this section, a different data set was used to construct validity, convergent validity, composite reli- ability, reliability analyses, correlation analysis, and network analysis.

#### 4.2.1. Participants and procedure A minimum sample size of 200 is recommended for factor analysis (Comrey & Lee, 2013). Study II’s participants consisted of 139 women (57.1%) and 104 men (42.8%) recruited through convenience sam- pling. These 243 participants were aged between 18 and 55 years (Mage ¼ 26.54, SD ¼ 7.79). The descriptive characteristics of the participants are displayed in Participant recruitment, inclu- sion, ethical approval and other procedures were similar to those in “Study I”. ##### 4.2.2. Measures 4.2.2.1. AI Anxiety Scale (AIAS). The scale was developed by Wang and Wang ([2022)](#about-the-authors) and adapted into Turkish by Akkaya et al. ([2021)](#ethical-approval). AI Anxiety Scale (AIAS) is a 16-item measurement tool to assess the AI anxiety (e.g., “I am concerned that an AI technique/product could be misused”). Participants rate each item on a seven-point scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). The scale comprises four dimensions: AI configuration, sociotechnical blindness, learning, and job replacement. Higher scores indicate greater AI anxiety. The reliability coefficient for AI anxiety was found to be 0.81, while the current study reported a reliability coefficient of 0.94 for AI anxiety.

##### 4.2.2.2. AI Acceptance Scale Short Form (AIAS-SF). The scale was originally developed by De Winter et al. (2024). The ChatGPT Acceptance Disposition Scale was modified and also adapted into Turkish by Batuk et al. ([2024)](#ethical-approval), resulting in the AI Acceptance Scale Short Form (AIAS-SF). This scale is a 6- item measurement tool to assess AI acceptance (e.g., “I find AI programmes useful for answering my questions”). Participants rate each item on a five-point scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). The scale comprises two dimensions: effectiveness and concerns. A high score reflects great AI acceptance. The reliability coefficient for AI acceptance was found to be 0.91, while the current study reported a reliability coefficient of 0.73.

#### 4.2.3. Statistical analysis The normality of AICAS items was assessed using the kurtosis and skewness criteria of ±2 (George & Mallery, 2019). Construct validity was examined by CFA, and model fit values (CFI, TLI, GFI, RMSEA, and

8 B. KAYA ET AL.

SRMR) above 0.90 were considered acceptable (Hoyle & Panter, 1995). An AVE value above 0.50 was used as the criterion for convergent validity and, a CR value above 0.70 for composite reliability (Hair et al., 2014). The factor loadings, item-total correlations, and reliability coefficients of the AICAS items were exam- ined. Criterion validity was analyzed using Pearson’s correlation coefficient and network analysis.

#### 4.2.4. Results The kurtosis values of the items ranged from −1.06 to −0.57, and the skewness values ranged from −0.31 to 0.34, indicating normality. First, as the CFA found model fit values within the acceptable range (v2/df ¼ 1.98; CFI ¼ 0.99; GFI ¼ 0.98, TLI ¼ 0.98; RMSEA ¼ 0.06; SRMR ¼ 0.02), construct val- idity was established for AICAS. Factor loadings ranged between 0.70 and 0.89, and item-total correla- tions were between 0.69 and 0.83. The AVE value of 0.67 supported convergent validity, and the CR value of 0.93 confirmed composite reliability. The internal consistency was obtained as a ¼ 0.93, x ¼ 0.93, and k6 ¼ 0.93. The factor loadings and item-total correlations of the AICAS items are pre- sented in [Table](#b-study-ii-values) [2,](#b-study-ii-values) and the CFA results are illustrated in [Supplemental](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [Appendix](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [B](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) (see [Figure](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [3B)](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913).

In this study, criterion validity was satisfied as AI competence anxiety was positively correlated with AI anxiety (r ¼ 0.72, p \< 0.05) and negatively correlated with AI acceptance (r ¼ −0.38, p \< 0.05). Furthermore, network analysis demonstrated both the connections between AICAS items and the rela- tionships between AI competence anxiety, AI anxiety, and AI acceptance. Correlation coefficients are presented in [Table](#433-statistical-analysis-each-step-in-the-analyses-followed-the-same-procedure-as-described-in-the-statistical-analysis-section-of-study-i-therefore-they-are-not-mentioned-here-to-avoid-repetition) [4,](#433-statistical-analysis-each-step-in-the-analyses-followed-the-same-procedure-as-described-in-the-statistical-analysis-section-of-study-i-therefore-they-are-not-mentioned-here-to-avoid-repetition) the links of the AICAS items are illustrated in [Figure](#441-participants-and-procedure-a-minimum-sample-size-of-200-is-recommended-for-factor-analysis-comrey--lee-2013-study-ivs-participants-consisted-of-128-women-571-and-96-men-429-recruited-through-convenience-sam--pling-these-224-participants-were-aged-between-18-and-52-years-mage--2567-sd--718-the-descriptive-characteristics-of-the-participants-are-displayed-in-table-1-participant-recruitment-inclu--sion-ethical-approval-and-other-procedures-were-similar-to-those-in-study-i-therefore-the-proce--dures-are-not-reported-here-to-avoid-repetition) [1,](#441-participants-and-procedure-a-minimum-sample-size-of-200-is-recommended-for-factor-analysis-comrey--lee-2013-study-ivs-participants-consisted-of-128-women-571-and-96-men-429-recruited-through-convenience-sam--pling-these-224-participants-were-aged-between-18-and-52-years-mage--2567-sd--718-the-descriptive-characteristics-of-the-participants-are-displayed-in-table-1-participant-recruitment-inclu--sion-ethical-approval-and-other-procedures-were-similar-to-those-in-study-i-therefore-the-proce--dures-are-not-reported-here-to-avoid-repetition) and the links of the varia- bles are depicted in Appendix B (see [Supplemental](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [Figure](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [4B)](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913).

### 4.3. Study III

In this section, the AIOS was developed. Accordingly, EFA, one of the CTT, and GRM, one of the IRT models, were used. A different dataset was used for this section. A Likert-type scale was developed to measure AI optimism, drawing on the optimism model (Carver & Scheier, [2002)](#ethical-approval) and following estab- lished protocols.

#### 4.3.1. Item generation Item development for the scale began with a detailed examination of the existing literature on AI opti- mism and attitudes toward AI. Key studies addressing these constructs were carefully reviewed (e.g., Grassini, 2023; Schepman & Rodway, 2020, 2023; Stein et al., [2024)](#about-the-authors), which informed the creation of an initial set of items. Based on this review, an initial item pool of 17 items was generated. To establish content validity, four subject matter experts—two specializing in measurement and evaluation and two in psychological counseling—were consulted. The experts assessed each scale item in terms of its rele- vance to the intended construct, using the categories of “appropriate, partially appropriate, and inappropriate”. This method aligns with Lawshe’s (1975) framework, which highlights the importance of expert judgment in determining item relevance during scale construction. Based on their feedback, the items were refined to better align with the intended constructs. Expert evaluations were used to examine the face and content validity of the scale. A final language check was carried out by a linguist proficient in both Turkish and English to enhance the overall clarity and consistency of the items. DeVellis (2017) emphasized that a limited number of items, a strong representation of the latent con- struct, and the careful selection of focal items all contribute to the scale’s overall usefulness. Therefore, in the EFA process, the items that best represent the latent construct were selected while minimizing the number of AIOS items. Following the integration of all feedback, the scale was finalized with 6 items, each measured on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

#### 4.3.2. Participants and procedure A minimum sample size of 200 is recommended for factor analysis (Comrey & Lee, 2013). Study III’s participants consisted of 214 women (67.9%) and 101 men (32.1%) recruited through convenience sam- pling. These 315 participants were aged between 18 and 57 years (Mage ¼ 22.64, SD ¼ 4.93). The descriptive characteristics of the participants are displayed in #### 4.3.4. Results The items’ kurtosis values were between −0.63 and 0.15, and the skewness values were between −0.59 and −0.11, which indicated normality. First, EFA was conducted. Since the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin value was 0.84, the sample size was sufficient for the 17-item pool. DeVellis (2017) emphasized that a limited number of items, a strong representation of the latent construct, and the careful selection of focal items all contribute to the scale’s overall usefulness. Therefore, in the EFA process, the items that best represent the latent con- struct were selected while minimizing the number of AIOS items. The AIOS six-item single-factor struc- ture was accepted as the eigenvalues were 3.29 for the first factor and 0.74 to 0.32 for the second and other factors. AIOS single-factor structure explained 54.86% variance. Factor loadings were between 0.66 and 0.79, commonalities were between 0.43 and 0.62, and item-total correlations were between 0.52 and 0.66. The scree plot also suggested a single-factor solution. Internal consistency was obtained with reliabil- ity coefficients of a ¼ 0.83, x ¼ 0.83, and k6 ¼ 0.82. The factor loadings, commonalities and item-total cor- relations of the AIOS items are presented in [Table](#433-statistical-analysis-each-step-in-the-analyses-followed-the-same-procedure-as-described-in-the-statistical-analysis-section-of-study-i-therefore-they-are-not-mentioned-here-to-avoid-repetition) [3](#433-statistical-analysis-each-step-in-the-analyses-followed-the-same-procedure-as-described-in-the-statistical-analysis-section-of-study-i-therefore-they-are-not-mentioned-here-to-avoid-repetition) and EFA results for the AIOS, and the Turkish and English versions of the scale are presented in [Supplemental](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [Appendix](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [A](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) (see [Tables](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [5A,](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [6A,](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913)and[7A)](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913).

Afterwards, the items’ discrimination was analyzed through GRM. Item 1 displayed medium dis- crimination (discrimination coefficient ¼ 1.32) while the remaining items displayed very high discrim- ination, with coefficients ranging from 1.86 to 2.75. Also, the boundary characteristic curves demonstrated the distinctiveness of the AIOS items. The discrimination coefficients of the AIOS items are presented in [Supplemental](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [Appendix](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [A](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) (see [Table](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [8A)](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) and the scree plot and the boundary charac- teristic curves are illustrated in [Supplemental](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [Appendix](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [B](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) (see [Figures](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [5B](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) and [6B)](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913).

##### 4.4.2. Measures 4.4.2.1. Digital Well-being Scale (DWS). Arslankara et al. ([2022)](#ethical-approval) developed the Digital Well-being Scale (DWS) as a 12-item measurement tool to assess digital well-being (e.g., “I can easily adapt to new tech- nologies”). Participants rate each item on a five-point scale ranging from 1 (doesn’t reflect at all) to 5 (fully reflective). It has three dimensions: digital satisfaction, safe and responsible behavior, and digital health. A high score reflects great digital well-being. The reliability coefficient of digital well-being (a ¼ 0.79) was found. The current study reported a reliability coefficient of digital well-being (a ¼ 0.75).

##### 4.4.2.2. AI self-efficacy Short Form (AISE-SF). The Technology Self-Efficacy Scale (AISE-SF) developed by Montag et al. (2023)was modified by Turk€ et al. ([in](#about-the-authors) [press)](#about-the-authors)and adapted into Turkish as AISE-SF. Thisscale is a 5-item measurement tool to assess AI self-efficacy (e.g., “I can easily use AI tools”). Participants rate each item on a seven-point scale ranging from 1 (do not agree at all) to 7 (completely agree). A high score on the unidimensional scale reflects greater AI self-efficacy. The reliability coefficient of AI self-efficacy (a¼ 0.77) was found. The current study reported a reliability coefficient of AI self-efficacy (a¼ 0.93).

### 4.5. Study V

In this section, the mediation of AI self-efficacy and AI optimism in the association between GenAI liter- acy and AI competence anxiety was examined using the AIOS and the AICAS, which were developed and validated in Studies I-IV. A different data set is used, and a relational research design wass employed to examine the non-causal relationship between dependent and independent variables (Creswell, 2008).

#### 4.5.1. Participants and procedure The Monte Carlo simulation tool (Schoemann et al., 2017) was used to determine the sample size for the serial mediation analysis. This tool requires a minimum of 312 participants for the two serial medi- ation model to display a power of 0.90 at 95% confidence level with 5,000 replications. Study V’s par- ticipants consisted of 424 women (59.1%) and 294 men (40.9%) recruited through convenience sampling. These 718 participants were aged between 18 and 66 years (Mage ¼ 26.34, SD ¼ 6.68). The descriptive characteristics of the participants are displayed in Participant recruitment, inclu- sion, ethical approval, and other procedures were similar to those in “Study I.” Therefore, the proce- dures are not reported here.

##### 4.5.2. Measures 4.5.2.1. Generative AI Literacy Scale (GenAILS). The AI Literacy Scale was developed by Wang et al. ([2023)](#about-the-authors) and modified and adapted into Turkish as the GenAILS by Gokc€ ¸earslan et al. (2024). GenAILS consists of 10 items (e.g., “I always follow ethical principles when using generative AI applications”) across four dimensions: ethics, awareness, use and evaluation. Participants rate each item on a five- point scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). A high score reflects great GenAI literacy. The reliability coefficient for GenAI literacy was found to be 0.74. The current study reported a reliability coefficient of GenAI literacy (a ¼ 0.79).

##### 4.5.2.2. AI Self-Efficacy Short Form (AISE-SF). The Technology Self-Efficacy Scale developed by Montag et al. (2023) was modified by Turk€ et al. ([in](#about-the-authors) [press)](#about-the-authors) and adapted into Turkish as AISE-SF. This scale is a 5-item measurement tool to assess AI self-efficacy (e.g., “I can easily use AI tools”). Participants rate each item on a seven-point scale ranging from 1 (do not agree at all) to 7 (completely agree). A high score on the unidimensional scale reflects greater AI self-efficacy. The reported reliability coefficient of AI self-efficacy was 0.77. The current study found a reliability coefficient of AI self-efficacy (a ¼ 0.74).

##### 4.5.2.3. AI Optimism Scale (AIOS). The validity and reliability assessments of the AIOS were carried out by Study I and Study II. Additionally, this study reported the reliability coefficient of AI Optimism (a ¼ 0.89).

##### 4.5.2.4. AI Competence Anxiety Scale (AICAS). The validity and reliability assessments of the AICAS were conducted by Study III and Study IV. Additionally, this study reported a reliability coefficient of

0.93 for AI Competence Anxiety.

##### 4.5.3. Statistical analysis Before conducting serial mediation analysis, normality, multicollinearity, and autocorrelation assump- tions were checked. Skewness and kurtosis values within ±2 indicated normality (George & Mallery, 2019). Multicollinearity was assessed using VIF \< 10 and tolerance \> 0.10, while the Durbin-Watson statistic between 1 and 3 indicated no autocorrelation of residuals (Field, 2017). Then, model 6 of PROCESS macro (Hayes, 2018) was used for serial analysis, and the significance of indirect effects was assessed by bootstrapping (5000 resamples) with a 95% confidence interval.

##### 4.5.4. Results 4.5.4.1. Preliminary analyses. Skewness values of the variables ranged from −0.38 to 0.21, and kurtosis values ranged from −0.88 to 0.31, indicating normality. VIF values between 1.19 and 1.41 and tolerance values between 0.71 and 0.84 showed no multicollinearity, while a Durbin-Watson value of 1.97 showed no autocorrelation between residuals. GenAI literacy was positively associated with AI self-efficacy (r ¼ 0.46, p \< 0.05) and AI optimism (r ¼ 0.39, p \< 0.05) and negatively associated with AI competence anxiety (r ¼ −0.17, p \< 0.05). AI self-efficacy was positively associated with AI optimism (r ¼ 0.26, p \< 0.05), and negatively associated with AI competence anxiety (r ¼ −0.21, p \< 0.05). Also, AI opti- mism was negatively associated with AI competence anxiety (r ¼ −0.36, p \< 0.05). Correlation and descriptive statistics are presented in [Table](#4523-ai-optimism-scale-aios-the-validity-and-reliability-assessments-of-the-aios-were-carried-out-by-study-i-and-study-ii-additionally-this-study-reported-the-reliability-coefficient-of-ai-optimism-a--089) [5.](#4523-ai-optimism-scale-aios-the-validity-and-reliability-assessments-of-the-aios-were-carried-out-by-study-i-and-study-ii-additionally-this-study-reported-the-reliability-coefficient-of-ai-optimism-a--089)

4.5.4.2. Serial mediation analysis. The bootstrapping analysis found that both AI self-efficacy (b ¼ −0.08, 95% CI ¼ \[−0.13, −0.03\]) and AI optimism (b ¼ −0.15, 95% CI ¼ \[−0.20, −0.10\]) mediated the relationship between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety. It also demonstrated the serial mediation role of AI self-efficacy and AI optimism in the association between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety (b ¼ −0.02, 95% CI ¼ \[−0.04, −0.01\]). Standardized indirect impacts are presented in [Table](#4523-ai-optimism-scale-aios-the-validity-and-reliability-assessments-of-the-aios-were-carried-out-by-study-i-and-study-ii-additionally-this-study-reported-the-reliability-coefficient-of-ai-optimism-a--089) [6,](#4523-ai-optimism-scale-aios-the-validity-and-reliability-assessments-of-the-aios-were-carried-out-by-study-i-and-study-ii-additionally-this-study-reported-the-reliability-coefficient-of-ai-optimism-a--089) standardized direct impacts are illustrated in Figure 3, and unstandardized direct impacts are presented in [Supplemental](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [Appendix](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [A](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) (see [Table](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913) [9A)](https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2025.2609913).

5. Discussion

The spread of AI technologies around the world has launched the AI era. Researchers have begun to develop many instruments to measure AI-related concepts. Accordingly, the need for a new, useful, and sufficient scale for measuring AI competence anxiety and AI optimism has prompted us to develop AIOS and AICAS. Furthermore, this study examined the mediating role of AI self-efficacy and AI opti- mism to clarify the mechanism underlying the relationship between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety. The findings of this study revealed that AIOS and AICAS are valid and reliable, and explored the mediating role of AI self-efficacy and AI optimism between AI literacy and AI competence anxiety. The results of the study are discussed in detail.

Studies I and II demonstrated that the AIOS is a valid and reliable instrument. In Study I, EFA sup- ported the single-factor structure of the AIOS, and high reliability values evidenced internal consist- ency. Additionally, IRT confirmed that the scale items exhibit high levels of discrimination. In Study II, CFA yielded model fit values that fell within the acceptable range, further confirming the AIOS’s single-factor structure. An AVE value within the acceptable range indicated that the scale demonstrated convergent validity, while a CR value within the acceptable range indicated composite reliability. High reliability values confirmed internal consistency. Moreover, AI optimism was positively correlated with digital well-being and AI self-efficacy, supporting criterion-related validity. All results showed that AIOS is a useful tool for measuring AI optimism.

Studies III and IV demonstrated that the AICAS is a valid and reliable instrument. In Study III, EFA supported the single-factor structure of the AICAS, and high reliability values evidenced internal consistency. Also, IRT confirmed that the AICAS items exhibit high levels of discrimination. In Study IV, CFA yielded model fit values that fell within the acceptable range, further confirming the AICAS’s single-factor structure. An AVE value in the acceptance range indicated that the scale demonstrated convergent validity, while a CR value in the acceptance range indicated composite reliability. High reli- ability values confirmed internal consistency. Furthermore, AI competence anxiety was positively corre- lated with AI anxiety and negatively correlated with AI acceptance, supporting criterion-related validity. All results showed that AICAS is a useful measure of AI competence anxiety.

In addition to developing the instruments, the study identified the mediating role of AI self-efficacy between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety. Consistent with this finding, previous studies have shown that AI literacy increases AI self-efficacy (Becirovic et al., [2025)](#ethical-approval) and AI self-efficacy reduces AI anxiety (Bewersdorff et al., [2025)](#ethical-approval). Furthermore, Karaoglan Yilmaz et al. (2025) demonstrated that digital competencies negatively affect AI anxiety through self-regulation abilities. The social cognitive theory offers a possible explanation for this finding. According to this theory, both direct and indirect learning contribute to supporting self-efficacy, and high self-efficacy, in turn, alleviates anxiety (Bandura, [1988)](#ethical-approval). AI literacy helps individuals recognize AI technologies, understand their beneficial

14 B. KAYA ET AL.

use, critically evaluate them, and be aware of potential ethical violations. This understanding promotes their self-efficacy regarding AI (Hornberger et al., 2025). AI self-efficacy supports the belief in an indi- vidual’s ability to use and manage AI technologies, thereby reducing anxiety toward AI (Chen et al., [2024a)](#ethical-approval). Additionally, GenAI literacy enables individuals to recognize GenAI, use it effectively, be aware of its shortcomings and advantages, and know the ethical boundaries. This knowledge supports AI self- efficacy and helps reduce anxiety.

This study demonstrated the mediation of AI optimism between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety. Compatible with this study’s findings, Hollands and Breazeal (2024) found that digital literacy increases optimism, and Johnstone et al. (2014) found that optimism reduces anxiety. Furthermore, the optimism model suggests that developing an individual’s competence and skills in a specific field enhances optimism, and high optimism buffers anxiety (Scheier & Carver, 2018). AI literacy fosters a positive attitude toward AI, enabling individuals to gain knowledge about AI technologies, to utilize them effectively, and to safeguard themselves from potential harm (Laupichler et al., 2024). Karaoglan Yilmaz and Yilmaz (2025) emphasize that individuals’ skills in performing uncertain and complex tasks related to GenAI foster a positive attitude toward its use. Positive expectations of GenAI promote its acceptance (Karaoglan Yilmaz et al., 2024). An individual’s positive attitude toward AI also alleviates concern about AI technologies (Cho & Seo, 2024). In this direction, GenAI literacy promotes positive perceptions and expectations of AI technologies, which supports AI optimism, and subsequently miti- gates AI anxiety. In other words, GenAI literacy alleviates AI anxiety by fostering AI optimism.

The current study lastly confirmed the serial mediation of AI self-efficacy and AI optimism in the asso- ciation between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety. The social cognitive theory presented a pos- sible interpretation of this finding. This theory suggests that an individual’s personal and environmental learning promotes belief in their abilities and positive expectations, which in turn protects against anxiety (Bandura, [1988)](#ethical-approval). High AI literacy supports AI self-efficacy as it helps individuals become aware of AI tech- nologies, use them effectively, and assess AI strengths and weaknesses (Bewersdorff et al., [2025)](#ethical-approval). High self- efficacy fosters optimism by promoting positive perceptions and expectations (Karademas et al., 2007), while elevated optimism, in turn, helps alleviate anxiety (Zenger et al., [2010)](#about-the-authors). Consequently, GenAI literacy strengthens individuals’ confidence in their ability to learn and manage AI technologies, while also foster- ing positive perceptions and expectations toward these technologies. This whole process mitigates their anxiety about their own competence toward AI. Put differently, GenAI literacy impacts AI competence anxiety by enhancing AI self-efficacy and AI optimism.

6. Implications

The current study demonstrated the validity and reliability of AIOS and AICAS. Accordingly, scholars may use AIOS to measure individuals’ AI optimism and AICAS to measure AI competence anxiety. Both scales can serve as practical tools for professionals to understand individuals’ AI optimism and AI compe- tence anxiety. Measuring AI optimism through AIOS and AI competence anxiety through AICAS can help implement targeted strategies. In this context, AICAS may help identify individuals who experience high levels of AI competence anxiety and prepare intervention programmes for them. Measuring AI opti- mism may also help prepare empowering programmes to increase positive perceptions and expectations of AI. AIOS and AICAS can be adapted and used in different cultures and groups.

This study gained deep insights into the roles of AI self-efficacy and AI optimism in the association between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety. In this context, a GenAI literacy-based psychoedu- cation programme can be prepared for individuals with high AI competence anxiety. Practitioners implementing this programme can support AI optimism and self-efficacy and alleviate AI competence anxiety. Casal-Otero et al. ([2023)](#ethical-approval) underlined that integrating AI literacy into K − 12 curriculum increases the benefits of AI while reducing potential harms. Furthermore, Southworth et al. ([2023)](#about-the-authors) sug- gest that an AI literacy curriculum will foster university students’ creativity and openness to innovation. In this respect, policymakers’ inclusion of GenAI literacy in the curriculum may increase AI self- efficacy and AI optimism, and buffer AI competence anxiety. Educators can conduct group activities and projects based on GenAI literacy, particularly those experiencing high AI competence anxiety. These GenAI literacy-based interventions can help increase AI self-efficacy and AI optimism, while

INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF HUMAN–COMPUTER INTERACTION 15

alleviating AI competence anxiety. Policymakers can organize seminars and workshops to enhance GenAI literacy, thereby supporting AI self-efficacy and AI optimism and reducing AI competence anx- iety. Similarly, digital designers can develop applications to improve GenAI literacy, including targeted tools for individuals experiencing high AI competence anxiety.

7. Limitations and future research

Although the current study employed both the CTT and IRT to develop AIOS and AICAS and examined serial mediation with the model, it has several limitations. First, nonrandom sampling limited generaliz- ability. Future researchers are encouraged to use random sampling to reduce the risk of sampling bias in scale development and mediation analysis. Second, although various reliability coefficients were reported for AIOS and AICAS, it was a limitation is that the long-term stability of the scales was not checked. Future studies may examine the test-retest reliability to evaluate the long-term stability of AIOS and AICAS. Third, factors related to AI (e.g., AI type, duration of AI use, and intention to use AI) and other contextual factors (e.g., family type, culture, socioeconomic status, occupation, and education) were over- looked in the development of AIOS and AICAS, as well as in the serial mediation model. Future research- ers are advised to consider contextual factors in the development of scales and the analysis of mediation models. Fourth, the development of the AIOS and AICAS and the examination of the serial mediation model were conducted in a single cultural context, limiting generalizability. Cross-cultural studies are rec- ommended to validate AIOS and AICAS and examine the serial mediation roles of AI self-efficacy and AI optimism between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety. Fifth, although a randomized control ques- tion was included in the surveys, the self-report scales remain limited by the possibility of participants responding in a socially desirable way. Future studies may diversify data collection methods, such as using a mixed-methods design and repeated measures. Sixth, the exclusion of the non-clinical population was a limitation. Future studies may examine the validity of AIOS, AICAS, and this study’sserial mediation model in a clinical population. Seventh, since the cross-sectional design limits causality, future research should consider using a longitudinal mediation design to explore the mediation role of AI self-efficacy and AI optimism between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety. Finally, while the serial mediation effect was significant, it was relatively small. Further research with larger samples and alternative designs is rec- ommended to confirm these findings and evaluate their practical implications. Although the current scales exhibit potential practical value, their application requires further field testing and validity assessment across diverse educational and professional contexts.

8. Conclusion

The current study developed AIOS and AICAS and established their initial validity. These scales make a significant contribution by enabling the measurement of AI optimism and AI competence anxiety. Further exploration of AI optimism and AI competence anxiety using AIOS and AICAS is encouraged. Moreover, this study demonstrated the serial mediation of AI self-efficacy and AI optimism in the relationship between GenAI literacy and AI competence anxiety. Thus, the study revealed that GenAI literacy reduces AI competence anxiety by promoting AI self-efficacy and AI optimism. The current study makes a signifi- cant contribution to the existing literature by suggesting that GenAI literacy-based strategies promote AI self-efficacy and optimism while alleviating AI competence anxiety. Considering that AI competence anx- iety is likely to increase over time, we recommend further investigation of its antecedents.

### About the authors

Bilal Kaya completed his doctoral education at C¸ukurova University, Department of Psychological Counseling and Guidance. His research focuses on behavioral addiction, positive psychology and artificial intelligence.

Sena Gume€ is an assistant professor in the Department of Psychological Counseling and Guidance at Istanbul Medipol University, Turkey. She received her PhD in Guidance and Psychological Counseling from Yıldız Technical University. Her research interests include digital technology use, artificial intelligence, addiction, student engagement in educational settings, and positive psychology.

Naif Ergun€ is an associate professor in the Department of Psychology at Mardin Artuklu University. His research focuses on human–technology interaction, behavioral addictions, identity development, migration, and minority studies. He conducts interdisciplinary research, publishes extensively, and teaches personality and social psych- ology while contributing to community-based psychological support and academic collaboration.
